items.question: What is NowBuild?
items.answer: NowBuild is an AI Marketing Agent Team for solo founders who have built a product but do not know how to grow or validate its market. The team shares product memory, calls professional Channel Skills, and continuously researches, creates, distributes, and reviews one 30-day campaign using real market feedback.

items.question: How is this different from ChatGPT?
items.answer: ChatGPT is useful for one-off answers or drafts. NowBuild coordinates multiple Agents that share product memory, a market hypothesis, channel plans, publishing progress, and real feedback while calling Channel Skills to keep the same campaign moving.

items.question: What are Channel Skills?
items.answer: Channel Skills are platform-specific execution playbooks. A Reddit Agent studies community context and real questions; a TikTok Agent prepares hooks, spoken scripts, and storyboards; an SEO Agent organizes keywords and content clusters around search intent. They share one market goal but never simply rewrite the same post everywhere.

items.question: Can NowBuild publish completely automatically?
items.answer: NowBuild prepares publish-ready work and assists with browser publishing where the platform allows it. Login, CAPTCHA, account authorization, media selection, community-rule checks, and final confirmation may still require you. NowBuild does not store your platform passwords or pretend those platform controls do not exist.

items.question: How do automated Directory submissions work?
items.answer: The Directory Agent first matches opportunities by product type, audience, and submission requirements. It then prepares descriptions, tags, assets, and form fields and executes supported submission flows. Each third-party platform still controls acceptance, timing, fees, and whether a backlink is provided.

items.question: Can 30 days guarantee users or revenue?
items.answer: No. NowBuild promises a continuous, recorded, reviewable market-validation process—not guaranteed traffic, rankings, users, or revenue. After 30 days, you should have channel performance, user response, reusable content, and the market signals needed for the next decision.

The paid plan assembles the full AI Marketing Agent Team and unlocks a 30-day Campaign, Channel Skills, daily content and execution tasks, Directory automation, publishing tracking, and weekly reviews.

posts.title: The Product Is Done. Now What? A 30-Day Roadmap for Your First Launch
posts.excerpt: Most builders don't get stuck on the product — they get stuck on the step after shipping. Here's a day-1-to-day-30 market action roadmap.
posts.author: NowBuild Team
posts.content:
You built a tool with AI over the weekend. The landing page is live. You shared it three times — 12 visitors in 7 days, zero signups. That's not a product problem. It's a rhythm problem.

## Why most first launches fall apart

It's not a lack of theory. It's three things compounding: not knowing what today's post should say (blank-page fear), not knowing which channel to bet on (channel paralysis), and posting into silence with no idea whether to continue (the feedback black hole).

## Week 1: Set strategy, publish your first batch

Answer three questions first: How is your product different from the alternatives? Where do your target users already hang out? How much time can you spend daily? Then pick 2–3 core channels and schedule week one's content.

## Week 2: Adjust your message based on reactions

Watch which content gets likes, comments, or DMs. Double down on formats that get reactions; change the angle on ones that don't. This is when you add direct outreach.

## Week 3: Double down on what works

Use day-7 and day-14 data to cut ineffective actions and concentrate your time on channels showing market signal.

## Week 4: Review and decide what's next

By day 30 you should be able to answer: Which channel works for me? Which content structure converts? Next month — go deeper or switch arenas?

## The key isn't perfection — it's rhythm

15–30 minutes a day for 30 days beats one explosive week followed by three silent ones. The market rewards whoever keeps showing up.

posts.title: How to Choose Your First Marketing Channel, by Product Type
posts.excerpt: Product Hunt, Twitter, Reddit, newsletters… too many channels is a first-time marketer's worst enemy. Here's how to subtract.
posts.author: NowBuild Team
posts.content:
The first rule of channel selection: don't pick the hottest one — pick the one your target users are already on. The second rule: at most 2–3 channels in your first month.

## Match channels to your product type

**Tools for consumers**: story-driven posts on visual platforms plus a direct-message funnel. The 'why I built this' side-project story is a natural fit.

**Tools for developers (global)**: build in public on Twitter/X plus a concentrated Product Hunt launch. Accumulate two weeks of content before PH — a cold-start PH launch usually sinks.

**Courses and consulting**: personal network plus long-form newsletters. These products convert on trust; a short conversion path beats broad reach.

**Open source**: README optimization plus a technical community launch. Your README is your landing page — polish it until it's understandable in 3 seconds before promoting anywhere.

## Signals that a channel is working

Within two weeks, look for three things: engagement on content (likes and comments), inbound DMs or link clicks, and at least one real usage or inquiry. All three missing? Consider switching. Any one present? Worth two more weeks.

## The most common mistake

Opening every channel at once. Each channel has its own format and cadence — running five at once means doing all five badly. Subtraction is the most important strategy of a first launch.

posts.title: How to Get Your First 100 Users Without Spending a Dollar on Ads
posts.excerpt: Paid ads can amplify an untested message during a first launch. Here are three zero-budget paths for finding your first 100 users.
posts.author: NowBuild Team
posts.content:
The point of your first 100 users isn't revenue — it's market feedback: is your positioning right, does your message land, does the product give people a reason to stay? Running ads at this stage means paying to amplify an unvalidated message.

## Path 1: Tell your own story

'Why I built this' gives a first launch a concrete, human starting point. Instead of listing features, describe the problem as you experienced it: what frustrated you, what you tried, and why you decided to build. Compare the response with your feature-led posts before deciding which format deserves more effort.

## Path 2: One-to-one outreach

List the people most likely to need your product — colleagues, people who asked related questions in communities, or users describing problems with an alternative. Message each person individually and explain why the product may be relevant. Avoid mass outreach, ask for candid feedback, and record the objections you hear.

## Path 3: Answer questions where users already gather

Reddit, Hacker News, and relevant Slack or Discord groups can reveal the language people use for the problem. Find a question your product genuinely helps answer, respond thoroughly, and disclose your connection if you mention the product. A useful answer can remain discoverable and create a natural route to your site.

## How much time per day

Choose a daily block you can sustain; 15–30 minutes is a practical starting point for one focused action, such as publishing one post, sending a few personal messages, or answering one question. Keep a simple log so you can compare actions and responses instead of relying on memory.

## When to consider paid ads

Consider testing paid acquisition after you can answer three questions with evidence: Which message earns qualified responses? Why do users stay? What is an activated user worth to the business? Until then, use direct conversations and organic publishing to refine the message.
